topics.name: Courts, Sources of Law & Erie Basics
terms: Concurrent jurisdiction
Both state and federal courts may hear the same type of case, so the plaintiff chooses.
Exclusive federal jurisdiction
Congress has allowed only federal courts to hear a type of case.
Article III, Section 2
The constitutional list of the kinds of cases federal courts may hear.
Rules Enabling Act
28 U.S.C. § 2072, letting the Supreme Court write procedural rules that cannot alter substantive rights.
Subject matter jurisdiction
A court’s power to hear the type of dispute at issue; it can’t be waived or conferred by consent.
Court of limited jurisdiction
A court that may hear only the categories of cases authorized to it, like a federal district court.
Certiorari
The Supreme Court’s discretionary review of a lower court decision.
Civil action
The single form of action under Rule 2, merging the old separate systems of law and equity.
Erie doctrine
In diversity cases, federal courts apply state substantive law and federal procedure.
Federal general common law
Judge-made law that federal courts applied under Swift v. Tyson until Erie rejected it.
Rules of Decision Act
28 U.S.C. § 1652, which Erie read to require federal courts to apply state law where federal law doesn’t govern.
Choice of law rules
Rules a court uses to decide which state’s substantive law governs a claim.
Forum shopping
Choosing a court in hopes of getting a more favorable rule.
Predictive approach
Where state law is unclear, a federal court asks what the state’s highest court would hold today.
Federal specific common law
Federal judge-made rules that survive Erie where strong federal interests require a federal rule.
cases: Swift v. Tyson
Federal courts in diversity cases could apply their own general common law.
Erie R.R. v. Tompkins
Federal courts in diversity cases must apply state substantive law.
Klaxon Co. v. Stentor
A federal diversity court applies the choice of law rules of the state where it sits.
mcq: Where are most American lawsuits litigated?
State trial courts of general jurisdiction handle the great majority of cases (Ch. 1).
Federal courts’ subject matter jurisdiction is:
Limited to categories Congress authorizes within Article III
Limited to cases involving the federal government
Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction (Ch. 1).
Who bears the burden of showing a federal court has subject matter jurisdiction?
The party seeking a federal forum must establish jurisdiction (Ch. 1).
Under the Rules Enabling Act, a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure may not:
Abridge, enlarge, or modify any substantive right
Can parties consent to federal subject matter jurisdiction that doesn’t otherwise exist?
Subject matter jurisdiction can’t be created by consent or waiver (Ch. 1).
Erie rejected federal general common law (Ch. 24).
Under Erie, a federal court hearing a state-law claim in diversity applies:
State substantive law and federal procedure
That is the core Erie principle (Ch. 24).
A main policy concern behind Erie was:
Forum shopping and unequal treatment of in-state and out-of-state parties
Swift let outcomes turn on which court system was chosen (Ch. 24).
Under Klaxon, a federal diversity court picks which state’s law applies by using:
The choice of law rules of the state where it sits
Klaxon extends Erie to choice of law (Ch. 24).
If a state’s highest court hasn’t clearly decided an issue, a federal diversity court should:
Predict how that court would rule today
Follow the most recent trial court opinion
The state supreme court predictive approach (Ch. 24).
After Erie, does any federal common law remain?
Yes, specific federal common law where federal interests require it
Erie ended general, not specific, federal common law (Ch. 24).
Rule 1 says the Federal Rules should be applied to secure:
The just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action
hypo: Ana sues Ben in federal court on a claim governed by state law. Their state’s supreme court has a rule on point, but the federal judge thinks a different rule is wiser. What should the judge do?
Apply the state supreme court’s rule
Apply a federal general common law rule
After Erie, federal courts in diversity must follow state substantive law (Ch. 24).

A diversity case is filed in federal court in State A. The claim has ties to States A and B. State A’s courts would use a choice of law rule pointing to State B’s law. Which law should the federal court apply?
State B’s, following State A’s choice of law rules
State A’s, because it’s the forum
Klaxon: use the forum state’s choice of law rules (Ch. 24).
A federal judge in a diversity case finds a 1950 state supreme court decision on point. Strong signals suggest that court would reject the rule today. What approach does the judge use?
Predict what the state supreme court would hold today, requiring strong evidence to depart
Two companies want to litigate a dispute in federal court. Neither diversity nor a federal question exists. They sign a stipulation consenting to federal jurisdiction. Result?
The court still lacks subject matter jurisdiction
Jurisdiction exists if the judge agrees
Jurisdiction exists if the amount exceeds $75,000
Subject matter jurisdiction can’t be conferred by agreement (Ch. 1).
A plaintiff could file her case in either state or federal court. She picks state court. Which concept describes her choice?
Both systems may hear the case (Ch. 1).
A proposed Federal Rule would change the elements a plaintiff must prove to win a state-law claim. What is the problem?
It would modify a substantive right, which the Rules Enabling Act forbids
Only Congress may write procedural rules
Federal Rules can’t apply in diversity cases
Under Swift v. Tyson, a federal judge in a diversity case ignores a state court’s common law rule and applies her own view of the general law. After Erie, is that allowed?
No, she must apply the state rule
Yes, if the issue is commercial
Erie: there is no federal general common law (Ch. 24).

topics.name: Diversity Jurisdiction
terms: Complete diversity
No plaintiff may share state citizenship with any defendant.
Domicile
Where a person lives with the intent to remain indefinitely; it fixes an individual’s state citizenship.
Principal place of business
A corporation’s nerve center, where its high officers direct and control its activities.
Amount in controversy
For diversity, the amount at stake must exceed $75,000, not counting interest and costs.
Legal certainty test
A good-faith claim over $75,000 suffices unless it is legally certain the plaintiff can’t recover that much.
Aggregation
Adding claims together to meet the amount; one plaintiff may add all claims against one defendant.
Alienage jurisdiction
Jurisdiction over suits between U.S. state citizens and citizens of a foreign country.
Time-of-filing rule
Citizenship is measured when the complaint is filed; later moves don’t matter.
Stateless person
A U.S. citizen domiciled abroad, who can’t be a party to a diversity case.
Unincorporated association
An entity like an LLC or partnership that takes the citizenship of every member.
mcq: Complete diversity and more than $75,000 in controversy
Exceeding $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs (Ch. 3).
A corporation is a citizen of:
Its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of business
Every state where it does business
The state where its shareholders live
A corporation’s principal place of business is usually:
Its nerve center, where high officers direct the business
Where it has the most employees
Where it makes the most sales
An LLC is a citizen of:
Every state where any of its members is a citizen
The state where its manager lives
Unincorporated entities take their members’ citizenship (Ch. 3).
To establish a new domicile, a person needs:
Physical presence plus intent to remain indefinitely
Both elements are required; the old domicile continues until then (Ch. 3).
When is citizenship for diversity measured?
A U.S. citizen domiciled in France sues a Texas citizen. Diversity?
No: she is not a citizen of any state
U.S. citizens domiciled abroad are stateless for § 1332 (Ch. 3).
Is interest on the claim counted toward the $75,000?
No, interest and costs are excluded
A legal representative of a decedent’s estate is a citizen of:
The same state as the decedent
The state where the estate is probated
Two plaintiffs each have separate $40,000 claims against one defendant. Can they combine them to meet the amount?
No, separate plaintiffs can’t aggregate separate claims
Aggregation is generally allowed only for one plaintiff against one defendant (Ch. 3).
hypo: Pat (Ohio) sues Dee (Ohio) and Ray (Indiana) in federal court on a state-law claim for $200,000. Is there diversity jurisdiction?
No, Pat and Dee are both Ohio citizens
Yes, the amount is high enough
Only over the claim against Ray
Complete diversity fails if any plaintiff shares citizenship with any defendant (Ch. 3).
Lu moves from Utah to Idaho for a two-month summer job, planning to return to Utah in the fall. She sues an Idaho citizen in July. Lu’s citizenship?
Utah, because she lacks intent to remain in Idaho
Domicile needs intent to remain indefinitely (Ch. 3).
Acme Inc. is incorporated in Delaware and its officers run the company from Chicago, Illinois. Most of its factories are in Ohio. Acme’s citizenship?
State of incorporation plus nerve center (Ch. 3).
Kim (Nevada) sues a Nevada-based business after filing, but when she filed she was domiciled in Oregon. A month later she moves to Nevada permanently. Diversity?
Jo (Idaho) sues an LLC organized in Delaware with its headquarters in Texas. One LLC member lives in Idaho. Diversity?
No, the LLC is also an Idaho citizen
Yes, Delaware and Texas are diverse
Yes, LLCs are treated like corporations
An LLC takes the citizenship of each member (Ch. 3).
Sam (Utah) sues Tia (Colorado) for $60,000 on one claim and $20,000 on an unrelated claim. Is the amount requirement met?
Yes, one plaintiff may aggregate all claims against one defendant
Only if both claims are federal
Max (Montana) sues Lee (Wyoming) asking for $90,000, though at trial he recovers only $30,000. Did the federal court have jurisdiction?
Yes, if the $90,000 claim was made in good faith
No, the recovery was too low
No, jurisdiction is lost after trial
The legal certainty test looks at the good-faith claim at filing (Ch. 3).
A citizen of Mexico sues a California citizen for $100,000 in federal court. What basis supports jurisdiction?
Suits between state citizens and foreign citizens qualify (Ch. 3).

topics.name: Federal Question Jurisdiction
terms: Arising under
The phrase in Article III and § 1331 describing federal question cases.
Well-pleaded complaint rule
A federal question must appear in the plaintiff’s own claim, not in a defense or the reply to one.
Creation test
A case usually arises under federal law when federal law creates the cause of action.
Embedded federal issue
A federal question inside a state-law claim that can support jurisdiction if necessary, disputed, substantial, and resolvable without upsetting the federal-state balance.
The statute giving district courts jurisdiction over civil actions arising under federal law.
The statute giving federal courts exclusive jurisdiction over patent and copyright claims.
The statute giving federal courts admiralty and maritime jurisdiction.
Saving to suitors clause
The part of § 1333 preserving state court remedies in many maritime cases.
Anticipated defense
A federal defense the plaintiff expects the defendant to raise; it doesn’t create federal jurisdiction.
mcq: Is there an amount in controversy requirement for § 1331?
Federal question cases have no amount requirement (Ch. 4).
Under the well-pleaded complaint rule, jurisdiction depends on:
The plaintiff’s claim as properly pleaded
Any federal issue in the case
The statute is read more narrowly than the Constitution (Ch. 4).
A federal counterclaim by the defendant:
Doesn’t make the case arise under federal law
Jurisdiction turns on the plaintiff’s complaint (Ch. 4).
Patent infringement claims can be heard in:
A state-law claim with an embedded federal issue arises under federal law only if the issue is:
Necessarily raised, actually disputed, substantial, and resolvable federally without upsetting the federal-state balance
Most federal question cases fit which test?
Federal law creates the cause of action
The defendant is a federal agency
The creation test covers most cases (Ch. 4).
hypo: Pia sues in federal court on a state-law claim. Her complaint adds that the defendant will probably argue a federal statute protects it, and that the statute doesn’t apply. Federal question jurisdiction?
No, an anticipated federal defense doesn’t count
Yes, a federal statute is mentioned
Yes, if the statute is important
Raj sues his former employer in federal court under a federal statute that gives workers a right to sue. Both are citizens of the same state, and he seeks $5,000. Jurisdiction?
Yes, federal law creates his claim
No, the amount is too small
§ 1331 has no diversity or amount requirement (Ch. 4).
A software company sues a competitor in state court for patent infringement. What should happen?
The state court lacks jurisdiction; patent claims are exclusively federal
The state court may hear it
It must be heard in admiralty
It can proceed if both parties consent
Lin sues in federal court on a state-law claim. The defendant answers with a federal-law counterclaim. Does the counterclaim supply federal question jurisdiction over the case?
Jurisdiction rests on the plaintiff’s complaint (Ch. 4).
A state-law claim turns on the meaning of a federal tax statute. The meaning is genuinely contested and important to the federal system, and few cases like it exist. Could it arise under federal law?
Yes, under the embedded federal issue test
No, the claim is created by state law, so never
Only if the parties are diverse
Grable allows jurisdiction in this narrow category (Ch. 4).
Two shipowners sue each other over a collision on navigable waters. Which statute most directly gives a federal court jurisdiction?
A plaintiff’s complaint states only a state-law claim. It mentions in passing that the parties once litigated a federal case. Federal question?
No, the claim itself isn’t federal
Yes, if the earlier case was in federal court
The claim must arise under federal law (Ch. 4).

topics.name: Removal
terms: Removal
A defendant’s transfer of a case from state court to the federal district court for the district where it is pending.
Notice of removal
The document a defendant files in federal court to remove a case, under § 1446(a).
Forum defendant rule
A diversity-only case can’t be removed if a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the forum state.
Rule of unanimity
All properly joined and served defendants must join in or consent to removal.
Thirty-day window
Each defendant has 30 days after receiving the initial pleading through service to remove.
One-year limit
A diversity case generally can’t be removed more than a year after it began unless the plaintiff acted in bad faith.
Remand
Sending a removed case back to state court.
The rule that a remand order is generally not reviewable on appeal.
Lets a defendant remove a case with a federal claim joined to unrelated state claims, which are then severed and remanded.
mcq: The federal district court for the district and division where the state case is pending
A motion to remand for a defect other than subject matter jurisdiction must be made within:
30 days after the notice of removal
If the federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction after removal, it must:
Remand at any time before final judgment
Can a federal court remand a case to state court and have its remand order appealed?
After the notice of removal is filed and given to the state court, the state court:
Proceeds no further unless the case is remanded
If a case isn’t removable when filed but later becomes removable, the defendant has:
30 days after receiving a paper showing it is removable
§ 1446(b)(3), subject to the one-year limit in diversity cases.
The forum defendant rule applies to cases removed based on:
A plaintiff who faces a counterclaim in state court can remove the case:
No, only defendants to the original action may remove
Only if the counterclaim is federal
hypo: Ann (Ohio) sues Bob (Kentucky) in Ohio state court on a state-law claim for $200,000. Bob is served Monday. Can Bob remove?
No, he is an out-of-state defendant
Only after the answer is due
Complete diversity, enough amount, and no forum defendant (Ch. 5).
Cal (Utah) sues Dana (Idaho) in Idaho state court for $150,000 on a state-law claim. Dana is served. Can Dana remove?
No, the forum defendant rule bars it
Only to a Utah federal court
Dana is an Idaho citizen sued in Idaho (Ch. 5).
Eve sues three defendants in state court on a federal claim. Two want to remove, but the third, who was properly served, refuses to consent. Can the case be removed?
No, all served defendants must consent
Yes, federal claims are always removable
A defendant removes 45 days after being served. The plaintiff moves to remand 20 days after the notice of removal. Result?
Remand: the removal was late and the motion was timely
No remand: the motion was too late
A timely objection to a procedural defect wins (Ch. 5).
A defendant removes late, and the plaintiff waits 60 days before objecting to the timing. Diversity jurisdiction otherwise exists. Result?
The case stays in federal court; the procedural objection was waived
Non-jurisdictional defects must be raised within 30 days (Ch. 5).

A diversity case was not removable when filed because a nondiverse defendant was in it. Eighteen months later, the plaintiff in good faith dismisses that defendant. Can the remaining defendant remove?
No, the one-year limit has passed
Yes, within 30 days of the dismissal
A case is removed, and the federal judge later realizes there was never complete diversity. Nine months have passed. What must happen?
Transfer to the court of appeals
Lack of subject matter jurisdiction can be raised any time before final judgment (Ch. 5).
A plaintiff files in state court in Boise, Idaho. To which court may the defendant remove?
The U.S. District Court for the District of Idaho
The district embracing the place where the case is pending (Ch. 5).

topics.name: Foundations of Personal Jurisdiction
terms: Personal jurisdiction
A court’s power to bind a particular defendant to its judgment.
In personam jurisdiction
Power over the defendant personally, supporting a judgment that can be enforced anywhere.
In rem jurisdiction
Power over property in the state to decide everyone’s rights in it.
Quasi in rem jurisdiction
Using property in the state as the basis for deciding a dispute unrelated to that property, limited to the property’s value.
Minimum contacts
The defendant’s ties to the forum that make a suit there consistent with due process.
Fair play and substantial justice
The fairness standard that a suit must not offend under International Shoe.
Due Process Clause
The Fourteenth Amendment provision that limits a state court’s personal jurisdiction.
Territorial power theory
Pennoyer’s view that a state’s power extends only to people and property within its borders.
Special appearance
Appearing only to challenge personal jurisdiction without submitting to it.
cases: Pennoyer v. Neff
State courts have power over persons and property within their borders; personal jurisdiction needed in-state service, consent, or appearance.
International Shoe Co. v. Washington
Due process requires minimum contacts so suit doesn’t offend fair play and substantial justice.
Shaffer v. Heitner
All assertions of jurisdiction, including quasi in rem, must satisfy International Shoe.
Hanson v. Denckla
The unilateral activity of others can’t create the defendant’s contacts; the defendant must purposefully avail itself.
mcq: Which constitutional provision limits state courts’ personal jurisdiction?
The Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause
Under Pennoyer, how could a state court obtain in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident?
Serve him while he was in the state, or by his consent or appearance
International Shoe shifted the focus to:
The defendant’s contacts with the forum and fairness
After Shaffer v. Heitner, quasi in rem jurisdiction:
Must satisfy the minimum contacts standard
Is always valid if property is in the state
A judgment based on quasi in rem jurisdiction is limited to:
The value of the attached property
The court’s power rests on the property (Ch. 6).
Whose contacts matter for personal jurisdiction?
Contacts must be created by the defendant itself (Ch. 6).
Personal jurisdiction, unlike subject matter jurisdiction, can be:
hypo: In 1870, a state court entered a money judgment against a nonresident who was never served in the state, never appeared, and owned no attached property there. Under Pennoyer, was the judgment valid?
No, the court lacked power over him
Yes, if the plaintiff lived there

A Delaware court seizes a nonresident’s shares of stock, which Delaware law deems located there, to hear a claim unrelated to the stock. The defendant has no other Delaware contacts. Valid after Shaffer?
No, quasi in rem jurisdiction now requires minimum contacts
Yes, the property is in the state
Yes, up to the stock’s value
A company’s customer moves to State X on her own and keeps paying the company by mail. The company has no other X contacts. Do the payments give X jurisdiction over the company?
No, the customer’s unilateral move doesn’t create the company’s contacts
Yes, if the plaintiff sues in X
A defendant’s employees regularly solicit orders in State Y, and the claim arises from that activity. Under International Shoe, is jurisdiction likely proper in Y?
Yes, there are systematic contacts related to the claim
No, the company isn’t incorporated in Y
No, it wasn’t served in Y
Only if Y is the plaintiff’s home
A nonresident defendant files a motion solely to contest personal jurisdiction. Has she consented to jurisdiction by appearing?
Only if she is a corporation
Raising the defense properly preserves it (Ch. 6).
A state court applies a statute that lets it hear any case against anyone in the world, regardless of contacts. What limits that statute?
State jurisdiction must satisfy due process (Ch. 6).

topics.name: Specific Jurisdiction
terms: Specific jurisdiction
Jurisdiction over claims that arise out of or relate to the defendant’s contacts with the forum.
Purposeful availment
The defendant’s deliberate choice to act in or direct activity at the forum.
Relatedness
The requirement that the claim arise out of or relate to the defendant’s forum contacts.
Reasonableness factors
Burden on the defendant, forum interest, plaintiff’s interest, efficiency, and shared state policies.
Stream of commerce
A theory of contacts based on products moving through distribution chains into the forum.
Stream of commerce plus
The view that the defendant must do more than know products will reach the forum, such as targeting it.
Effects test
Jurisdiction may rest on intentional conduct expressly aimed at the forum and causing harm there.
Foreseeability
Not enough by itself; the defendant must reasonably anticipate being haled into the forum’s court.
Haled into court
The phrase describing what a defendant should reasonably anticipate when it has forum contacts.
cases: World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson
Foreseeability that a product will end up in a state isn’t enough; the defendant must reasonably anticipate suit there.
Burger King v. Rudzewicz
Deliberately created long-term obligations with a forum party can satisfy purposeful availment.
Asahi Metal v. Superior Court
Exercising jurisdiction over a foreign component maker was unreasonable; the Court split on stream of commerce.
Walden v. Fiore
Contacts must be with the forum itself, not just with a plaintiff who lives there.
Ford Motor v. Montana Court
‘Relate to’ doesn’t require strict causation between the contacts and the claim.
Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Superior Court
Nonresidents’ claims lacking any forum connection can’t ride on residents’ similar claims.
mcq: Is foreseeability that a product could end up in the state enough?
Arise out of or relate to the defendant’s forum contacts
Be filed where the plaintiff lives
Does ‘relate to’ require that the contacts caused the claim?
No, but a strong connection is needed
Who bears the burden of showing jurisdiction would be unreasonable once contacts and relatedness exist?
The defendant, with a compelling case
Which is NOT a reasonableness factor?
The factors listed in World-Wide and Burger King (Ch. 7).
Under the stream of commerce plus view, a manufacturer needs:
Conduct aimed at the forum, like marketing there
Only awareness its products reach the forum
Contacts with a plaintiff who lives in the forum, without other forum ties, are:
Enough if the harm is large
hypo: A New York dealer sells a car to New York residents, who drive it to Oklahoma, where it breaks down. The dealer does no business in Oklahoma. Can an Oklahoma court exercise specific jurisdiction over the dealer?
No, there was no purposeful availment of Oklahoma
Yes, the claim arose in Oklahoma
Only if the dealer is served there

A Florida company signs a 20-year franchise deal with a Michigan businessman, who agrees to send payments to Florida and follow Florida-directed rules. Can Florida exercise jurisdiction over him in a dispute about the deal?
Yes, he deliberately created ongoing obligations with Florida
No, he never went to Florida
A Nevada resident sues a Georgia officer in Nevada. The officer’s conduct all happened in Georgia, and he knew only that the plaintiff lived in Nevada. Jurisdiction in Nevada?
No, his contacts were with the plaintiff, not Nevada
Yes, the harm was felt in Nevada
Yes, if he is served by mail

A carmaker advertises, sells, and services its models throughout Montana. A Montana resident sues over a model the company first sold in another state, which was later resold into Montana. Jurisdiction in Montana?
Yes, the claim relates to the carmaker’s Montana market activity
No, the car wasn’t first sold in Montana
Only if the plaintiff bought it new

Out-of-state plaintiffs join California residents to sue a drug company in California. The nonresidents didn’t buy, use, or get hurt by the drug in California. Jurisdiction over the nonresidents’ claims?
No, their claims lack a California connection
Yes, the residents’ claims cover them
Yes, the company sells a lot in California
Only if the cases are consolidated

A foreign parts maker sells valves to a foreign assembler, knowing some finished products reach California. It doesn’t advertise or design for California. A dispute between the two foreign companies is brought in California. Most likely result?
Jurisdiction depends only on the amount
Asahi: all justices agreed it was unreasonable on those facts (Ch. 7).
A writer in Florida writes an article about a California resident, aimed at California readers, knowing the harm would be felt there. Jurisdiction in California?
Likely yes, under the effects test
No, the writer never went to California
No, only the publisher may be sued
Only if the article was printed in California
Conduct expressly aimed at the forum (Ch. 7).

A company in Idaho sells products only online to customers who find its site. It ships one order to Maine after a Maine buyer places it. A suit about that order is brought in Maine. What is the key question?
Whether the company purposefully availed itself of Maine
Whether the buyer lives in Maine
Whether the website is visible in Maine
Internet contacts still turn on purposeful availment (Ch. 7).

topics.name: General, Tag & Consent Jurisdiction
terms: General jurisdiction
Jurisdiction over any claim against a defendant, even one unrelated to its forum contacts.
At home
The standard for general jurisdiction: contacts so continuous and systematic the defendant is essentially at home.
Paradigm forums
For a corporation, its place of incorporation and principal place of business; for an individual, domicile.
Tag jurisdiction
Jurisdiction based on serving an individual while physically present in the forum.
Consent
Agreeing to a court’s jurisdiction, by agreement, conduct, or failing to object.
Forum selection clause
An agreement choosing the court where disputes between the parties will be litigated.
Waiver of personal jurisdiction
Losing the defense by not raising it in the first Rule 12 response.
Registration statute
A state law requiring out-of-state companies doing business there to register, sometimes as consent to jurisdiction.
cases: Goodyear Dunlop Tires v. Brown
General jurisdiction requires affiliations so continuous and systematic the corporation is essentially at home.
Daimler AG v. Bauman
Doing substantial business in a state doesn’t make a corporation at home there.
Burnham v. Superior Court
Serving an individual while voluntarily present in the state supports jurisdiction.
Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute
A forum selection clause in a form ticket was enforceable when fundamentally fair.
Perkins v. Benguet Mining
A company temporarily run from the forum could be subject to general jurisdiction there.
mcq: Where is a corporation always subject to general jurisdiction?
Its state of incorporation and principal place of business
Where is an individual subject to general jurisdiction?
Does large-scale business in a state make a corporation at home there?
Only if sales exceed half its total
Service on an individual while voluntarily present in the forum
General jurisdiction differs from specific jurisdiction because:
The claim need not relate to the forum contacts
A defendant can consent to personal jurisdiction by:
A forum selection clause, or by not objecting in time
A state statute treating registration to do business as consent to general jurisdiction
Jurisdiction based only on internet sales
Quasi in rem jurisdiction without contacts
hypo: Pat, a Texas resident, flies to California for a weekend conference and is handed a summons in a California suit unrelated to the trip. Can California exercise jurisdiction?
No, he has no minimum contacts
Only if he owns property there
A German carmaker’s U.S. subsidiary sells many cars in California. Plaintiffs sue the German parent in California over events that happened in Argentina. General jurisdiction in California?
No, the parent is not at home there
Acme is incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters in Texas. A plaintiff sues Acme in Texas over a dispute that happened entirely in Oregon. Jurisdiction in Texas?
Yes, general jurisdiction where Acme is at home
No, the claim arose in Oregon
Principal place of business is a paradigm forum (Ch. 8).
A passenger’s ticket says all disputes must be litigated in Florida. She sues the cruise line in Washington. The cruise line moves based on the clause. Likely result?
The clause is enforced if fundamentally fair
The clause is void because it’s on a form
The clause only applies to the cruise line
A defendant files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion but doesn’t raise lack of personal jurisdiction. Later she moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Result?
She may raise it at trial
A business is incorporated in Idaho with headquarters in Idaho. It is sued in Idaho over an incident in Nevada. Does Idaho need specific jurisdiction?
Yes, the claim arose in Nevada
Yes, unless the plaintiff lives in Idaho

topics.name: Notice, Service & Long-Arm Statutes
terms: Summons
The court document, issued by the clerk, that tells a defendant to appear and defend.
Service of process
Formal delivery of the summons and complaint to the defendant.
Waiver of service
Under Rule 4(d), a defendant’s agreement to skip formal service, earning extra time to answer.
Abode service
Leaving papers at the defendant’s dwelling with someone of suitable age and discretion who lives there.
Rule 4(m)
The 90-day deadline to serve after filing, extended for good cause.
Mullane standard
Notice must be reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform parties of the action.
Long-arm statute
A state statute that authorizes its courts to exercise jurisdiction over nonresidents.
Enumerated-act statute
A long-arm statute listing specific activities that support jurisdiction.
Due process long-arm
A long-arm statute reaching as far as the Constitution allows.
Rule 4(k)(1)(A)
Federal courts generally use the personal jurisdiction reach of the state where they sit.
mcq: Under Rule 3, a federal civil action is commenced by:
Filing a complaint with the court
Who may serve a summons and complaint?
Any nonparty who is at least 18
How long does a plaintiff have to serve after filing?
A defendant who waives service gets how long to answer?
60 days from when the request was sent (90 if outside the U.S.)
If a defendant refuses to waive service without good cause, the court must:
Make it pay the expenses of formal service
Which is NOT a proper way to serve an individual under Rule 4(e)(2)?
Mailing the papers to the defendant’s workplace
Leaving it at the defendant’s home with a suitable resident
Mail isn’t a Rule 4(e)(2) method, though state law methods are allowed under 4(e)(1).
A state court can exercise personal jurisdiction only if:
A long-arm statute authorizes it and due process allows it
Due process allows it, whatever the statute says
A long-arm statute that lists specific acts is called:
Ch. 9; Idaho Code § 5-514 is an example of a statute listing acts.
Due process requires notice that is:
Reasonably calculated to inform the parties
hypo: Ray files his complaint on March 1 but doesn’t serve the defendant until August 15, with no reason for the delay. What may the court do?
Dismiss without prejudice or order service within a set time
A process server leaves the summons with the defendant’s 16-year-old son at the home where they both live. Is that likely proper?
Likely yes, if the son is of suitable age and discretion
No, only adults 21 and up count
No, it must be handed to the defendant
The plaintiff herself hands the summons and complaint to the defendant. Proper?
No, the server must not be a party
A state’s long-arm statute covers only defendants who transact business in the state. The defendant didn’t transact business there but has enough contacts for due process. Jurisdiction?
No, the statute doesn’t authorize it
Notice of a case affecting many people is given only by newspaper ads, though the plaintiff knows the mailing addresses of some of them. Is that enough for those people?
No, mail notice is required for known addresses
Yes, if run for four weeks
A federal court in Idaho hears a state-law claim. How does it decide whether it has personal jurisdiction over the out-of-state defendant?
Apply Idaho’s long-arm statute and due process
Ask whether the defendant is a U.S. citizen
Personal jurisdiction doesn’t apply in federal court
A plaintiff sends a waiver request. The defendant signs and returns it. When is the answer due?
60 days after the request was sent

topics.name: Venue
terms: Venue
The statutory choice of which district within a court system is a proper place for trial.
Residential venue
Venue in a district where any defendant resides, if all defendants reside in that state.
Transactional venue
Venue in a district where a substantial part of the events or property at issue is located.
Fallback venue
Under § 1391(b)(3), any district with personal jurisdiction over a defendant, used only if no other district works.
Natural person’s residence
For venue, the district where the person is domiciled.
Entity defendant’s residence
For venue, any district where the entity is subject to personal jurisdiction for that action.
The statute defining venue and explaining it isn’t a jurisdictional requirement.
Waiver of venue
Losing a venue objection by not raising it in the first Rule 12 response.
mcq: Is venue a matter of subject matter jurisdiction?
Under § 1391(b)(1), venue is proper in a district where:
Any defendant resides, if all defendants reside in the same state
Does the plaintiff’s residence make venue proper under § 1391(b)?
Section 1391(b) looks at defendants and events (Ch. 11).
Can there be more than one proper venue?
Only if no district satisfies (b)(1) or (b)(2)
A corporate defendant resides, for venue, in:
Any district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction for that action
A defendant who isn’t a U.S. resident may be sued:
Does § 1391 govern venue in cases removed from state court?
No, removal goes to the district where the state case was pending
hypo: Dee lives in the Northern District of California. Eli lives in the Southern District of California. Both are sued together. Where is residential venue proper?
Either the Northern or Southern District of California
Nowhere, because they live in different districts
Fay (Oregon) and Gus (Idaho) are sued together. The events happened in the District of Utah. Where is venue proper?
No residential venue since they live in different states; transactional venue in Utah (Ch. 11).
A plaintiff from the District of Idaho sues an Ohio defendant in Idaho. All events happened in Ohio. Is venue proper in Idaho?
Yes, because the plaintiff lives there
Neither residence nor events point to Idaho, and the fallback doesn’t apply because Ohio works (Ch. 11).
The events in a case took place partly in Nevada and partly in Arizona, each substantially. Where is transactional venue proper?
In both the Nevada and Arizona districts
A ‘substantial part’ can occur in more than one district (Ch. 11).
A defendant answers without objecting to venue, then later moves to dismiss for improper venue. Result?
Venue can be raised any time
A corporation is sued in a district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction for that case. Is venue proper under § 1391(b)(1) if it is the only defendant?
Yes, it resides there for venue
No, it must be incorporated there
Only if the events happened there

topics.name: Transfer & Forum Non Conveniens
terms: § 1404(a) transfer
Moving a case from a proper venue to another district for convenience and in the interest of justice.
§ 1406(a) transfer
Dismissing, or transferring in the interest of justice, a case filed in an improper venue.
Transferor court
The court that sends a case away.
Transferee court
The court that receives a transferred case.
Forum non conveniens
Dismissal when a far more convenient forum, usually in another country, is available.
Adequate alternative forum
A forum where the defendant is amenable to process and the plaintiff has some remedy.
Private interest factors
Convenience factors like access to proof, availability of witnesses, and cost of trial.
Public interest factors
Factors like court congestion, local interest in the dispute, and familiarity with the governing law.
Law travels with the case
After a § 1404(a) transfer, the transferee court applies the law the transferor court would have applied.
cases: Piper Aircraft v. Reyno
Less favorable law in the foreign forum doesn’t ordinarily defeat dismissal for forum non conveniens.
Gulf Oil v. Gilbert
Forum non conveniens balances private and public interest factors.
Van Dusen v. Barrack
After a § 1404(a) transfer, the transferor court’s choice of law rules still apply.
Goldlawr v. Heiman
A court may transfer under § 1406(a) even if it lacks personal jurisdiction over the defendant.
mcq: Section 1404(a) transfer applies when venue in the original court is:
Under § 1404(a), a case may be transferred to a district where:
It might have been brought, or to which all parties have consented
Can a federal court transfer a case to a state court or foreign court?
Transfer is within the federal system; forum non conveniens handles other forums (Ch. 12).
When a case is filed in an improper venue, the court may:
Dismiss it, or transfer it if justice requires
A forum non conveniens dismissal requires:
A foreign plaintiff’s choice of a U.S. forum usually gets:
Less deference than a domestic plaintiff’s home choice
After a defendant’s § 1404(a) transfer, which court’s choice of law rules apply?
hypo: A case is properly venued in the District of Idaho, but nearly every witness and document is in the District of Oregon, where it could have been filed. What motion fits?
Venue is proper, so convenience transfer applies (Ch. 12).
A case is filed in a district where venue is improper. The statute of limitations has now run, so a dismissal would end the claim. What should the court consider?
Transferring under § 1406(a) in the interest of justice

Scottish families sue a U.S. aircraft maker in Pennsylvania over a crash in Scotland. Scottish law is less favorable to them. Most witnesses and evidence are in Scotland. Likely result on a forum non conveniens motion?
Dismissal in favor of Scotland is likely
Denial, because Scottish law is less favorable
Transfer to a Scottish federal court
A defendant moves to transfer a case from Mississippi to Pennsylvania under § 1404(a). Mississippi’s choice of law rules would apply Mississippi law. After transfer, what law applies?
The law the Mississippi court would have applied
A plaintiff sues in a district with proper venue but no personal jurisdiction over the defendant. Can the court transfer the case rather than dismiss?
Yes, a transfer is allowed even without personal jurisdiction
A defendant asks a U.S. federal court to send a case to a court in Japan. What doctrine is the right vehicle?
Federal courts can’t transfer to foreign courts (Ch. 12).

topics.name: Pleading
terms: Complaint
The pleading that starts a civil action by stating the plaintiff’s claims.
Rule 8(a)
Requires a short and plain statement of jurisdiction, of the claim showing entitlement to relief, and a demand for relief.
Plausibility standard
Well-pleaded facts must make it plausible, not just possible, that the plaintiff is entitled to relief.
Conclusory allegation
A bare legal conclusion that isn’t assumed true when testing a complaint.
Notice pleading
The liberal approach of the Federal Rules: give fair notice of the claim and its grounds.
Rule 9(b)
Requires that allegations of fraud or mistake be stated with particularity.
Caption
The heading of a pleading naming the court, the parties, the file number, and the type of pleading.
Pleading in the alternative
Stating claims or defenses alternatively or inconsistently, which Rule 8(d) allows.
Demand for relief
The part of a complaint stating what the plaintiff seeks, such as money or an injunction.
Rule 7(a)
The closed list of pleadings: complaint, answer, answers to counterclaims, crossclaims, and third-party complaints, and a court-ordered reply.
cases: Bell Atlantic v. Twombly
A complaint must state enough facts to make a claim plausible, retiring the ‘no set of facts’ test.
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
The plausibility standard applies to all civil actions; conclusions aren’t assumed true.
mcq: Which is NOT required by Rule 8(a)?
A list of all evidence the plaintiff will offer
A short and plain statement of jurisdiction
A short and plain statement of the claim
A demand for the relief sought
Under Iqbal, step one of reviewing a complaint is to:
Then ask whether the remaining facts make the claim plausible (Ch. 13).
At the pleading stage, well-pleaded factual allegations are:
May a plaintiff plead inconsistent claims?
Intent and knowledge may be alleged generally (Ch. 13).
Numbered, each limited as far as practicable to one set of circumstances
hypo: A complaint says only: ‘Defendant violated my rights and is liable to me.’ It gives no facts. Will it survive a motion to dismiss?
No, it is conclusory and states no plausible claim
Yes, if the amount is stated

A complaint alleges detailed facts showing the employer fired the plaintiff because of her age, in violation of a federal statute. The defendant says the facts aren’t true. On a motion to dismiss, the court:
Assumes the facts true and asks if they plausibly show a right to relief
Decides who is telling the truth
Dismisses because the facts are disputed
A plaintiff isn’t sure which of two defendants is responsible, so she alleges that one or the other is liable. Allowed?
A complaint alleges that the defendant ‘engaged in fraud’ without saying what was said, by whom, or when. What rule is the problem?
Fraud must be pleaded with particularity (Ch. 13).
A complaint omits any statement of the grounds for federal jurisdiction. What’s missing?
Parallel conduct by competitors is alleged, with nothing suggesting an agreement. The claim requires an agreement. Plausible?
No, parallel conduct alone is consistent with lawful behavior
Yes, discovery will fill the gaps
Only if the plaintiff is a business

topics.name: Care & Candor: Rule 11
terms: Rule 11(b)
By presenting a paper, a lawyer certifies proper purpose, legal support, factual support, and supported denials.
Reasonable inquiry
The investigation of facts and law a lawyer must make before presenting a paper.
Safe harbor
The 21 days a party has to withdraw or fix a challenged paper before a Rule 11 motion may be filed.
Improper purpose
Filing a paper to harass, cause unnecessary delay, or needlessly increase cost.
Nonfrivolous argument
A good-faith argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law, or for new law.
Show-cause order
A court’s order directing a lawyer or party to explain why conduct didn’t violate Rule 11.
Deterrence
The purpose of Rule 11 sanctions, which are limited to what suffices to deter repetition.
Makes a lawyer who unreasonably and vexatiously multiplies proceedings personally pay the excess costs.
Signature requirement
Every pleading, written motion, and other paper must be signed by an attorney of record or a party without a lawyer.
mcq: Pleadings, written motions, and other papers presented to the court
Discovery is covered by Rule 26(g), not Rule 11.
Before filing a Rule 11 motion, the movant must:
Serve it and wait 21 days for the paper to be withdrawn or corrected
The main purpose of Rule 11 sanctions is:
Factual contentions must have evidentiary support or:
Be specifically identified as likely to have support after discovery
Can a court raise Rule 11 on its own?
Yes, by ordering the lawyer to show cause
A represented party can’t be ordered to pay money sanctions for:
Signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating it
Absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm is:
Held jointly responsible for its lawyer’s violation
Responsible only if a partner signed
hypo: A lawyer files a complaint without talking to any witnesses or reading any documents, relying only on the client’s angry two-sentence email. The claims turn out baseless. Problem?
Yes, she didn’t make a reasonable inquiry
No, she can rely on her client entirely
No, Rule 11 doesn’t apply to complaints
Only if the case went to trial
A defendant serves a Rule 11 motion on the plaintiff. Ten days later, the plaintiff withdraws the challenged claim. Can the defendant now file the motion?
No, the claim was withdrawn within the 21-day safe harbor
A lawyer argues in good faith that a state supreme court decision should be overruled. The argument loses. Rule 11 violation?
No, it’s a nonfrivolous argument to change the law
A lawyer files a motion only to delay a hearing so his client can move assets. The motion has some legal support. Rule 11 problem?
Only if the hearing is canceled
A lawyer files proper discovery requests but they’re excessive and harassing. Does Rule 11 govern?
A lawyer repeatedly files duplicative motions to drive up the other side’s fees. Besides Rule 11, what statute may make him personally pay the excess costs?
After filing, a lawyer learns a key factual allegation is false but keeps arguing it at a hearing. Is that a problem?
Yes, later advocating counts as presenting
No, Rule 11 looks only at filing
No, there’s no duty to correct

topics.name: Responding to the Complaint & Default
terms: Answer
The defendant’s pleading responding to each allegation and stating defenses.
Rule 12(b) motion
A pre-answer motion raising defenses like lack of jurisdiction, improper venue, or failure to state a claim.
Failure to state a claim
Rule 12(b)(6): even if the allegations are true, the law gives no relief.
Affirmative defense
A defense the defendant must plead under Rule 8(c), such as the statute of limitations.
Waivable defenses
Personal jurisdiction, venue, process, and service of process, waived if left out of the first Rule 12 response.
Motion for a more definite statement
Rule 12(e): asks for a clearer pleading when one is too vague to respond to.
Motion to strike
Rule 12(f): removes redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter.
Judgment on the pleadings
Rule 12(c): a ruling based on the pleadings once they are closed.
Entry of default
The clerk’s notation under Rule 55(a) that a party failed to plead or otherwise defend.
Default judgment
A judgment against a party who has defaulted, entered by the clerk for a sum certain or otherwise by the court.
mcq: When is an answer generally due after service?
Filing a Rule 12 motion changes the answer deadline to:
14 days after the court rules on the motion
Which defense can never be waived?
Failure to state a claim may be raised:
In a pleading, by Rule 12(c) motion, or at trial
If matters outside the pleadings are considered on a 12(b)(6) motion, it is treated as a:
An allegation the defendant fails to deny (other than the amount of damages) is:
A defendant who lacks knowledge enough to admit or deny an allegation should:
Say so, which has the effect of a denial
The clerk may enter a default judgment when the claim is:
For a sum certain against a defendant who never appeared
An entry of default may be set aside for:
Rule 55(c); a default judgment is set aside under Rule 60(b).
Differ in kind from or exceed the amount demanded in the complaint
hypo: Dana moves to dismiss for improper venue only. The court denies the motion. In her answer, she now raises lack of personal jurisdiction. Result?
The personal jurisdiction defense is waived
It is timely in the answer
She may raise it at trial
A defendant answers and doesn’t raise failure to state a claim. At trial, she moves for judgment on that ground. Allowed?
Yes, failure to state a claim is preserved through trial
After two years of litigation, the court realizes the parties aren’t diverse and no federal claim exists. Nobody objected earlier. What must the court do?
Dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
A complaint is so vague that the defendant can’t tell what she is accused of doing. What motion fits best?
Rule 12(e) motion for a more definite statement
A defendant is served and does nothing for two months. The claim is for a sum certain of exactly $50,000. The defendant never appeared. What can happen?
The clerk enters default and may enter judgment for the sum certain
The plaintiff must go to trial
A complaint demands $20,000. The defendant defaults. At the damages hearing, the plaintiff proves $40,000. How much can the default judgment award?
A defendant’s answer says, ‘Defendant denies each and every allegation,’ though she knows several are true. Problem?
Yes, a general denial is proper only if she in good faith denies all allegations
No, general denials are always allowed
No, the plaintiff must prove everything anyway
Only if the complaint was verified
A defendant moves to dismiss for failure to state a claim and attaches a long affidavit with new facts. The judge considers it. How must the judge treat the motion?
As a summary judgment motion, giving both sides a chance to present material

topics.name: Amending Pleadings
terms: Amendment as a matter of course
Under Rule 15(a)(1), one amendment allowed without permission within set time limits.
Leave to amend
Court permission under Rule 15(a)(2), freely given when justice so requires.
Relation back
Treating an amended claim as filed on the original date for statute of limitations purposes.
Conduct, transaction, or occurrence
The test for relation back: the new claim arises from the same events set out in the original pleading.
Changing the party
Relation back for a new defendant requires notice and that it knew or should have known it would have been sued but for a mistake.
Amendment to conform to the evidence
Rule 15(b) amendment for issues tried by consent or raised at trial.
Supplemental pleading
Rule 15(d) pleading adding events that happened after the original pleading.
Futility
A reason to deny leave: the amendment couldn’t survive a motion to dismiss.
Scheduling order deadline
After it passes, a party must show good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) to amend.
cases: Krupski v. Costa Crociere
For relation back against a new party, the question is what the new defendant knew, not what the plaintiff knew.
mcq: A party may amend once as a matter of course within:
21 days after serving it, or 21 days after a responsive pleading or certain Rule 12 motions
After that period, a party may amend with:
The opposing party’s written consent or the court’s leave
The standard for granting leave to amend is:
Freely given when justice so requires
Only for good cause shown by clear evidence
Which is a common reason to deny leave to amend?
Undue delay, bad faith, prejudice, or futility
An amended claim relates back if it arises out of:
The same conduct, transaction, or occurrence as the original pleading
For relation back against a newly named defendant, notice must come within:
The Rule 4(m) period for serving the original complaint
Must be approved by the jury
Events after the date of the pleading being supplemented
hypo: Ana files her complaint. Ten days later, before any response, she wants to add a claim. Does she need permission?
No, she may amend once as a matter of course
Yes, she needs the court’s leave
Yes, she needs the defendant’s consent
Ben’s claim arises from a warehouse fire. After the limitations period runs, he amends to add a new legal theory based on the same fire. Does it relate back?

Cara sues ‘Costa Cruise Lines’ but the right defendant is its related company ‘Costa Crociere,’ which learned of the suit within the 4(m) period and knew she meant to sue the ship’s operator. Limitations has run. Relation back?
Yes, the new defendant knew it would have been sued but for her mistake
No, Cara should have known the right name
No, new parties never relate back
A plaintiff moves to amend two years into the case, the day before trial, adding new claims needing new discovery. Likely result?
Leave may be denied for undue delay and prejudice
At trial, the plaintiff offers evidence on an issue not in the pleadings. The defendant doesn’t object and fully litigates it. What happens to the issue?
It is treated as if raised in the pleadings
It is waived by the plaintiff
A plaintiff wants to add a new claim arising from a totally separate event that happened after limitations ran. Would it relate back?
No, it doesn’t arise from the same occurrence
A scheduling order set a deadline for amendments, which has passed. A party now seeks to amend. What must it show first?
Good cause to modify the schedule

topics.name: Joinder of Claims & Parties
terms: Rule 18 claim joinder
A party may join as many claims as it has against an opposing party, related or not.
Compulsory counterclaim
A counterclaim arising from the same transaction or occurrence as the opposing claim, lost if not asserted.
Permissive counterclaim
Any counterclaim not arising from the same transaction or occurrence.
Crossclaim
A claim against a coparty arising from the same transaction or occurrence; never compulsory.
Permissive party joinder
Rule 20 joinder of parties when claims share a transaction or occurrence and a common question.
Impleader
Rule 14: a defendant brings in a nonparty who is or may be liable to it for all or part of the claim against it.
Third-party defendant
The nonparty brought into a case by impleader.
Misjoinder
Improper joinder of parties, which Rule 21 says isn’t a ground for dismissing the action.
Logical relationship test
A common test for whether claims arise from the same transaction or occurrence.
Severance
Splitting claims or parties into separate proceedings, such as under Rule 21.
mcq: Rule 18 lets a party join against an opposing party:
Any claims it has, related or not
Joinder rules don’t supply jurisdiction, though (Ch. 17).
A compulsory counterclaim that isn’t asserted is:
Generally barred in a later suit
A common transaction or occurrence and a common question of law or fact
Without leave, a defendant may implead a third party within:
14 days after serving its original answer
Impleader is proper when the third party:
Is or may be liable to the defendant for all or part of the claim against it
Is solely liable to the plaintiff instead
Rule 14(a)(1); ‘it’s him, not me’ isn’t impleader (Ch. 17).
Not a ground for dismissing the action
Each joined claim still needs its own basis for subject matter jurisdiction
Jurisdiction doesn’t matter for joined claims
Only the first claim needs jurisdiction
hypo: Pia sues Dan over a car crash. Dan believes Pia caused the crash and wants to recover for his own losses from it. He waits and files a separate suit later. Likely problem?
His claim was a compulsory counterclaim and is now barred
He must refile it as a crossclaim
Pia sues Dan over a crash. Dan has an unrelated claim against Pia from a separate business dispute years ago. May he assert it in this case?
Three passengers on the same bus are injured in one crash. Can they sue the bus company together?
Only if their damages are equal
Pia sues Dan and Eve. Dan believes Eve is responsible for any loss and wants to recover from her in the same case. What is Dan’s claim against Eve?
Pia sues Store. Store says that if it is held liable, Supplier is liable to Store for all or part of that amount. Supplier isn’t a party. What can Store do?
Supplier may be liable to Store for the claim (Ch. 17).
Pia sues Store. Store argues only that Supplier, not Store, caused the problem, and Store owes nothing at all. Can Store implead Supplier on that theory?
No, impleader requires derivative liability to the defendant
Yes, any responsible party may be impleaded
‘It’s him, not me’ is a defense, not impleader (Ch. 17).
A plaintiff joins two defendants whose claims arise from unrelated events. The court finds misjoinder. What should it do?
Drop a party or sever the claims, not dismiss the action
Store impleads Supplier. Supplier wants to assert a claim against Pia arising from the same events. Allowed?
No, third-party defendants can only defend

topics.name: Complex Joinder: Rule 19, Intervention & Interpleader
terms: Required party
A person who must be joined if feasible under Rule 19(a).
Joinder if feasible
Joining a required person when she can be served and joinder won’t destroy subject matter jurisdiction.
Rule 19(b) factors
Prejudice, ways to lessen it, adequacy of a judgment without the person, and whether the plaintiff has another forum.
Intervention of right
Rule 24(a): a nonparty with an interest that may be impaired, not adequately represented, may join.
Permissive intervention
Rule 24(b): a nonparty with a claim or defense sharing a common question may be allowed to join.
Adequate representation
If an existing party adequately protects the applicant’s interest, intervention of right may be denied.
Interpleader
A suit by a stakeholder that brings all claimants to a fund or property into one case.
Stakeholder
The party holding the disputed fund or property in interpleader.
Statutory interpleader
28 U.S.C. § 1335 interpleader: minimal diversity, $500 or more, and nationwide service.
Rule interpleader
Rule 22 interpleader, which needs an ordinary basis for jurisdiction.
mcq: A person is required under Rule 19(a)(1)(A) if:
Without her, the court can’t accord complete relief among the existing parties
She is related to a party
If a required party can’t be joined, the court:
Weighs the Rule 19(b) factors to decide whether to proceed or dismiss
A timely motion, an interest that may be impaired, and inadequate representation
A claim or defense sharing a common question of law or fact with the main action
An interest that will be impaired
Minimal diversity among claimants and $500 or more
A key advantage of statutory interpleader is:
Rule 22 interpleader in a diversity case requires:
Complete diversity between stakeholder and claimants and more than $75,000
hypo: An insurer holds $100,000 under a policy. Claimants from Ohio, Ohio, and Idaho each say the money is theirs. The insurer is from Ohio. Can it use statutory interpleader?
Yes, minimal diversity exists among the claimants
No, the insurer shares citizenship with claimants
No, the amount is too high
Using the same facts, could the insurer use Rule 22 interpleader based on diversity?
No, complete diversity between it and the claimants is lacking
A plaintiff sues over title to land she co-owns with her sister. The sister isn’t joined, and a ruling could impair her rights in the land. Is the sister a required party?
Only if she lives in the forum
A required party can’t be joined because her joinder would destroy diversity. The plaintiff has another forum, state court, where everyone can be joined. Likely result?
The court may dismiss after weighing Rule 19(b) factors
The court must ignore the absent party
The court must join her anyway
The court transfers to state court
A neighborhood group wants to intervene in a suit over a permit. The city, a party, already makes every argument the group would make. Intervention of right?
Likely denied: its interest is adequately represented
A company moves to intervene in a case that has been in trial for three weeks. Its interest was clear from the start. Likely result?
Timeliness is required under both 24(a) and (b) (Ch. 18).
A nonparty’s claim shares a common legal question with a pending case but its interest wouldn’t be impaired. Which intervention route is available?
Permissive intervention, in the court’s discretion

topics.name: Supplemental Jurisdiction
terms: Supplemental jurisdiction
Federal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 over claims lacking their own basis but related to a claim that has one.
Same case or controversy
The § 1367(a) standard: the claims share a common nucleus of operative fact.
Common nucleus of operative fact
The Gibbs test: claims a plaintiff would ordinarily be expected to try together.
Anchor claim
The claim with an independent basis for federal jurisdiction.
In diversity-only cases, bars supplemental claims by plaintiffs against persons joined under Rules 14, 19, 20, or 24 when inconsistent with § 1332.
Lets a court decline supplemental jurisdiction, such as when all anchor claims are dismissed.
Tolls the limitations period for a dismissed supplemental claim while pending and for 30 days after dismissal.
Pendent claim
The older name for a related state claim joined to a federal claim.
cases: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs
Related state claims sharing a common nucleus of operative fact may be heard with a federal claim.
Owen Equipment v. Kroger
A plaintiff can’t assert a claim against a nondiverse third-party defendant in a diversity case.
Exxon Mobil v. Allapattah
If one diverse plaintiff meets the amount, § 1367 covers co-plaintiffs’ smaller claims.
mcq: Form part of the same case or controversy as the anchor claim
Section 1367(b) restricts supplemental jurisdiction mainly over claims by:
A court may decline supplemental jurisdiction when:
All claims with original jurisdiction have been dismissed
If a court declines supplemental jurisdiction, the limitations period is:
Tolled while pending and for 30 days after dismissal
Can § 1367 be used to destroy complete diversity among original parties?
A compulsory counterclaim in a federal case usually falls within:
Do § 1367(b)’s limits apply in federal question cases?
No, only when jurisdiction rests solely on diversity
hypo: Pia sues her employer under a federal statute and adds a related state-law claim from the same firing. Both are from the same state. Can the federal court hear the state claim?
Pia (Iowa) sues Owen (Nebraska) in a diversity case. Owen impleads Kroger (Iowa). Pia then asserts a state claim against Kroger. Supplemental jurisdiction?
In the same case, can Owen’s impleader claim against Kroger (Iowa) be heard under supplemental jurisdiction?
Yes, § 1367(b) restricts plaintiffs’ claims, not defendants’
No, Kroger is nondiverse from Pia
Two diverse plaintiffs sue a diverse defendant over the same events. One claims $100,000, the other $30,000. Can the federal court hear the $30,000 claim?
No, it is below the amount
A federal claim is dismissed early. Only a related state claim between nondiverse parties remains. What may the court do?
Decline supplemental jurisdiction and dismiss the state claim
A plaintiff’s federal claim concerns one event in March. She adds a state claim about an unrelated event in July. Supplemental jurisdiction?
No, they don’t share a common nucleus of operative fact
Yes, any claim can be added
A state claim is dismissed under § 1367(c) on the last day of its limitations period. How long does the plaintiff have to refile in state court?

topics.name: The Scope of Discovery
terms: Scope of discovery
Any nonprivileged matter relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case.
Proportionality
Weighing the issues, amount at stake, access to information, resources, importance, and burden versus benefit.
Admissibility
Information need not be admissible in evidence to be discoverable.
Privilege
A rule protecting confidential communications, like lawyer-client, from discovery and trial.
Privilege log
A description of withheld materials that lets others assess a privilege claim, under Rule 26(b)(5)(A).
Work product
Documents and tangible things prepared in anticipation of litigation by or for a party.
Opinion work product
A lawyer’s mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, and legal theories, given near-absolute protection.
Substantial need and undue hardship
The showing required to get ordinary work product.
Protective order
A Rule 26(c) order, on good cause, protecting a party from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue burden.
Consulting expert
A retained expert who won’t testify, discoverable only in exceptional circumstances.
Testifying expert
An expert expected to testify, whose opinions may be discovered and who may be deposed.
Reasonable inquiry before filing
Rule 11 assumes informal investigation before the complaint is filed.
cases: Hickman v. Taylor
A lawyer’s witness statements and notes prepared for litigation are protected work product.
mcq: To be discoverable, information must be:
Nonprivileged, relevant to a claim or defense, and proportional
Does information have to be admissible to be discoverable?
Who usually bears the burden of showing a request is disproportionate?
Do the Federal Rules create privileges?
No, Rule 26 recognizes privileges created elsewhere
Materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, not the underlying facts
Ordinary work product can be obtained by showing:
Substantial need and inability to get the equivalent without undue hardship
A party withholding documents as privileged must:
Expressly claim the privilege and describe what is withheld
A protective order requires a showing of:
Facts and opinions of a non-testifying retained expert are discoverable:
Only on a showing of exceptional circumstances
hypo: A defendant refuses to produce relevant emails, arguing they’d be inadmissible hearsay at trial. Is that a valid objection to discovery?
No, discoverable information need not be admissible
Yes, inadmissible material is never discoverable
After an accident, a company’s lawyer interviews witnesses and writes memos with her own thoughts on the case. The other side asks for the memos. Likely result?
Protected work product; her opinions get near-absolute protection
The other side asks: ‘What facts do you know about the accident?’ The company says the facts are work product because its lawyer gathered them. Valid?
No, the underlying facts aren’t protected
Work product protects documents, not facts (Ch. 21).
A key witness gave a statement to the defendant’s investigator right after the event and has since died. The plaintiff asks for the statement. Likely result?
Discoverable on a showing of substantial need and undue hardship
Discoverable only if it helps the defendant
In a $20,000 case, the plaintiff demands every email the defendant company has sent in ten years, costing $500,000 to produce. What objection fits?
A defendant hires an expert just to advise its lawyers. She won’t testify. Can the plaintiff depose her?
Yes, all experts can be deposed
Yes, if she wrote a report
A party seeks discovery of a witness’s embarrassing private medical history that has little to do with the claims. What can the witness’s side request?
Good cause to protect from embarrassment (Ch. 21).

topics.name: Discovery Tools & Case Management
terms: Initial disclosures
Information parties must provide without a request under Rule 26(a)(1), like witnesses and documents they may use.
Rule 26(f) conference
The parties’ meeting to plan discovery, held before most discovery may begin.
Scheduling order
A Rule 16(b) order setting deadlines for joining parties, amending, discovery, and motions.
Deposition
Sworn oral questioning of a party or witness under Rule 30, recorded for later use.
Rule 30(b)(6) deposition
A deposition of an organization, which must designate people to testify on listed topics.
Interrogatories
Written questions to another party, answered under oath, limited to 25 under Rule 33.
Request for production
A Rule 34 request to inspect documents, electronically stored information, or things.
Physical or mental examination
A Rule 35 exam ordered for good cause when a party’s condition is in controversy.
Request for admission
A Rule 36 request to admit facts or the genuineness of documents; unanswered requests are deemed admitted.
Subpoena
A Rule 45 order compelling a nonparty to testify or produce documents.
Duty to supplement
Under Rule 26(e), a party must correct or complete incomplete disclosures and responses.
Final pretrial order
An order shaping trial that can be modified only to prevent manifest injustice.
mcq: Before the Rule 26(f) conference, parties generally:
May not seek discovery from any source
Must file motions for summary judgment
Without waiting for a discovery request
Without leave or agreement, each side may take how many depositions?
A deposition is limited, absent agreement or order, to:
A party gets how many interrogatories without leave?
To get documents from a nonparty, use:
A court order on good cause, with the condition in controversy
If a party doesn’t answer a request for admission within 30 days, the matter is:
Hold pretrial conferences and issue scheduling orders
Judges can’t coerce settlement or stipulations (Ch. 26).
A final pretrial order can be modified only:
hypo: A plaintiff sends interrogatories the day after filing the complaint, before any conference with the defendant. Must the defendant answer now?
No, discovery generally waits for the Rule 26(f) conference
A plaintiff wants testimony from the defendant corporation about its safety policies but doesn’t know which employee knows. What tool fits?
The organization must designate a witness (Ch. 22).
A plaintiff serves 40 interrogatories without permission. How many must the defendant answer?
It may object beyond 25; leave or agreement is needed for more
A plaintiff claims a permanent back injury. The defendant wants its own doctor to examine her. What is needed?
A court order for good cause under Rule 35
A defendant ignores a request to admit that a letter is genuine for 45 days. What happens?
A party wants records held by a nonparty bank. What tool works?
A Rule 34 request to the bank
A Rule 30(b)(6) notice to the bank as a party
A party learns its initial disclosure listed the wrong witness. What must it do?
Supplement or correct it in a timely way
A judge orders a party to stipulate to facts it disputes, threatening sanctions. Proper?
No, judges can’t force parties to stipulate or settle
Yes, if the facts are obvious
A party wants to call a witness at trial who was left out of the final pretrial order. What must it show?
That excluding the witness would cause manifest injustice

topics.name: Voluntary Dismissal & Summary Judgment
terms: Notice of dismissal
A plaintiff’s unilateral dismissal before the defendant serves an answer or summary judgment motion.
Two-dismissal rule
A second notice dismissal of the same claim operates as an adjudication on the merits.
Dismissal by court order
A Rule 41(a)(2) voluntary dismissal on terms the court sets.
Involuntary dismissal
A Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute or comply, usually an adjudication on the merits.
Without prejudice
A dismissal that allows the plaintiff to sue again.
Summary judgment
Judgment without trial when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
Material fact
A fact that could affect the outcome under the governing substantive law.
Genuine dispute
A dispute where a reasonable jury could find for the nonmoving party.
Partial summary judgment
Summary judgment on part of a claim or defense, or on some claims.
Rule 56(d)
Lets a nonmovant who can’t yet present essential facts seek more time for discovery.
cases: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett
A movant without the burden of proof may point to the absence of evidence supporting the nonmovant’s case.
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby
A dispute is genuine if a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.
mcq: A plaintiff may dismiss by notice, without a court order, before the defendant serves:
An answer or a summary judgment motion
A dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, improper venue, or failure to join a required party is:
Not an adjudication on the merits
Doesn’t weigh evidence or judge credibility
The court views the evidence in the light most favorable to:
Which facts are ‘material’ is determined by:
A movant who won’t bear the burden of proof at trial can win by:
Disproving an element or showing the nonmovant lacks evidence of one
A summary judgment motion may be filed, by default, until:
30 days after the close of all discovery
A dispute about the law alone:
hypo: A plaintiff files suit, then files a notice of dismissal before the defendant answers. Later she refiles the same claim. Allowed?
Yes, the first notice dismissal is without prejudice
No, the dismissal was with prejudice
The same plaintiff dismisses the refiled federal case by notice again, then files a third time. Result?
The second notice dismissal operated as an adjudication on the merits
After the defendant has answered, the plaintiff wants out of the case without the defendant’s agreement. What must she do?
Move for a dismissal by court order under Rule 41(a)(2)
A plaintiff ignores court orders and doesn’t prosecute her case for a year. The court dismisses under Rule 41(b), saying nothing more. Can she refile?
Generally no, it operates as an adjudication on the merits
On summary judgment, two witnesses give sworn conflicting accounts of whether the light was red. The color is material. Can the court grant summary judgment?
No, there is a genuine dispute of material fact
Yes, if one witness seems more credible
The defendant moves for summary judgment, showing the plaintiff has no evidence on an element she must prove at trial. The plaintiff responds only with her pleadings’ allegations. Likely result?
Celotex; the nonmovant must point to evidence (Ch. 27).
Facts are undisputed, and the parties disagree only about how a statute should be read. Can summary judgment be granted?
Yes, a legal dispute alone doesn’t require trial
The nonmovant shows by affidavit that the key evidence is in the movant’s files and discovery hasn’t happened yet. What may the court do?
Defer or deny the motion, or allow time for discovery under Rule 56(d)

topics.name: Judgment as a Matter of Law & New Trials
terms: Judgment as a matter of law
Rule 50 judgment when no reasonable jury would have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for a party.
Directed verdict
The traditional name for a Rule 50(a) motion made during trial.
JNOV
Judgment notwithstanding the verdict, the old name for a renewed Rule 50(b) motion.
Renewed motion
A Rule 50(b) motion after the verdict, allowed only if a 50(a) motion was made first.
New trial
A Rule 59 order setting aside a verdict and trying the case again.
Against the weight of the evidence
A new trial ground where the verdict is seriously erroneous, though some evidence supports it.
Remittitur
Offering the winner a choice between a reduced award and a new trial.
Additur
Raising a jury award as an alternative to a new trial, not allowed in federal court.
Rule 60(b)
Lets a court relieve a party from a final judgment for listed reasons, like excusable neglect or a void judgment.
Clerical mistake
An error in the record that Rule 60(a) lets the court fix at any time.
mcq: A Rule 50(a) motion may be made:
Any time before the case is submitted to the jury, after the opponent has been fully heard on the issue
A reasonable jury would have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for the party
The judge agrees with the jury
When ruling on JMOL, the judge:
Views the evidence for the nonmovant and doesn’t judge credibility
A Rule 50(b) renewed motion must be filed no later than:
Can a party file a Rule 50(b) motion without first moving under 50(a)?
The 50(b) motion renews the earlier motion (Ch. 29).
A new trial motion must be filed within:
On a weight-of-the-evidence new trial motion, a judge:
May weigh the evidence, unlike on JMOL
Must defer completely to the jury
Motions under Rule 60(b)(1)–(3) must be made within a reasonable time and no more than:
A judgment void for lack of jurisdiction may be challenged under:
hypo: After the plaintiff rests, the defendant moves for JMOL, arguing the plaintiff offered no evidence at all on an essential element. If that’s right, what should the judge do?
The defendant never moved under Rule 50(a). The jury finds for the plaintiff. The defendant now files a Rule 50(b) motion. Result?
It must be denied: a 50(a) motion is a prerequisite
The court may grant it anyway
A jury awards $2 million for an injury the evidence shows is worth at most $500,000. What can the judge offer?
A remittitur: accept a reduced amount or face a new trial
A jury awards $5,000 when the plaintiff’s undisputed losses are $50,000. Can a federal judge simply raise the award?
No, additur isn’t allowed; a new trial is possible
Yes, with the defendant’s consent only
Some evidence supports the verdict, but the judge firmly believes it is seriously wrong and a miscarriage of justice. JMOL or new trial?
New trial on the weight of the evidence
JMOL isn’t available when a reasonable jury could find as it did (Ch. 31).
Two weeks after judgment, the clerk notices the judgment lists the wrong amount by a typo. What rule fixes it?
Clerical mistakes can be fixed any time (Ch. 31).
Eighteen months after judgment, a party discovers new evidence it couldn’t have found earlier. Can it get relief under Rule 60(b)(2)?
No, the one-year limit has passed
Yes, if the evidence is strong
A defendant’s lawyer missed the answer deadline because of a sudden hospitalization, and the defendant moves promptly after default judgment. Which ground fits?

topics.name: Appeals & Scope of Review
terms: Final judgment rule
Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, courts of appeals generally review only final decisions.
Final decision
A decision that ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing to do but execute the judgment.
Interlocutory order
A ruling made before final judgment.
